description_full: Astronics Corporation, through its subsidiaries, designs and manufactures products for the aerospace, defense, and electronics industries in the United States, rest of North America, Asia, Europe, South America, and internationally. It operates in two segments, Aerospace and Test Systems. The Aerospace segment offers lighting and safety systems, electrical power generation systems, distribution and seat motions systems, aircraft structures, avionics products, systems certification, and other products. This segment serves airframe manufacturers (OEM) that build aircraft for the commercial transport, military, and general aviation markets; suppliers to OEMs; and aircraft operators, such as airlines; suppliers to the aircraft operators; and branches of the U.S. Department of Defense. The Test Systems segment designs, develops, manufactures, and maintains automated test systems that support the aerospace and defense, communications, and mass transit industries, as well as training and simulation devices for commercial and military applications. This segment serves OEMs and prime government contractors for electronics and military products. The company was incorporated in 1968 and is headquartered in East Aurora, New York.

financial_summary: Astronics Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $2.5B market cap on $862M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +17% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.

Returns on capital run at -2% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 22% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $43M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.55× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 3.2× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 8.5×.
Shareholder yield is only 0.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.
